formula: estimate = starting premium × index(new) ÷ index(start), where index = driver and area factors × (liability share × limits × vehicle liability + damage share × deductible × loan or lease × vehicle age × vehicle damage)
changelogNote: Factors now come from public sources where we could find them: state insurance-department price surveys (Oklahoma, North Dakota, District of Columbia), North Carolina's accident surcharge rule, ISO loss costs, and HLDI losses by make and model. Everything else is labeled as our estimate and widens the range. The separate teen switch is gone; the 16–18 age band is the teen factor.

driver-age.title: Driver age
driver-age.note: The main driver's age. 16–18 is the teen factor; there is no separate teen switch.

16-18.derivation: Oklahoma 2026, Scenario A (age 16, single, drives to school, under 7,500 miles) ÷ Scenario D (age 55, married, commutes, 12,000 miles). Same company, city, and sex; median 4.507 (middle half of companies 3.210–5.409; 351%) over 200 comparisons. Rough because the two profiles also differ in marital status, use, and mileage. The teen is the only driver on their own policy; adding a teen to a parent's policy is priced differently.

19-21.derivation: Oklahoma 2026, Scenario B (age 21, single) ÷ Scenario D (age 55, married); same commute, mileage, car, and coverage. Same company, city, and sex; median 1.918 (middle half of companies 1.687–2.058; 92%) over 200 comparisons. Rough because marital status also differs.

22-25.derivation: District of Columbia 2024, age 25 ÷ age 39 (same company, same group: married, single female, single male; state-minimum coverage), median 1.170 (middle half of companies 1.097–1.313; 17%) over 87 comparisons, times the 26–39 factor above (age 39 is in that band).

26-39.derivation: Oklahoma 2026, Scenario C (age 36) ÷ Scenario D (age 55): both married, 18-mile round-trip commute, 12,000 miles, same car and coverage. Same company, city, and sex; median 1.109 (middle half of companies 1.059–1.196; 11%) over 200 comparisons.

65+.derivation: District of Columbia 2024, age 66 ÷ age 39 (same company and group; state-minimum coverage), median 0.939 (middle half of companies 0.839–1.028; -6%) over 87 comparisons, times the 26–39 factor above.

driving-experience.title: Years licensed
driving-experience.note: Only used from age 22. For younger drivers the age factor already covers being new.

10+.label: Licensed 10 or more years
10+.derivation: The starting point for years licensed.

under-1.label: Licensed under 1 year (age 22 and up)
under-1.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. Newly licensed adults usually pay more than experienced drivers of the same age.

1-3.label: Licensed 1–3 years (age 22 and up)
1-3.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. A smaller version of the new-driver effect.

4-9.label: Licensed 4–9 years (age 22 and up)
4-9.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. Some insurers keep a small new-driver charge for several years.

not-used.label: Not used under 22
not-used.derivation: For drivers under 22 the age factor already covers being a new driver, so years licensed is not counted again.

driving-record.title: Driving record
driving-record.note: At-fault accidents in the last three years.

clean.label: Clean
clean.derivation: The starting point for driving record.

one.label: One at-fault accident
one.derivation: North Carolina's Safe Driver Incentive Plan, set by state law, adds 40% for an at-fault accident with $2,300 or less of property damage (1 point), 55% for $2,300–$3,850 (2 points), and 70% for $3,850 or more or bodily injury over $1,800 (3 points). Typical claims today are above $3,850, so we use 70%, with 40% as the low edge. Rough because other states' insurers set their own surcharges.

two-or-more.label: Two or more at-fault accidents
two-or-more.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. Two North Carolina 3-point accidents would total 6 points; the NC page does not list the surcharge for 6 points, so we added two single-accident surcharges (1 + 0.70 + 0.70). The low end is one accident; the high end is the largest surcharge on the NC table (12 points, +340%).

7500-15000.label: 7,500–15,000 miles a year
7500-15000.derivation: The starting point for yearly mileage.

under-7500.label: Under 7,500 miles a year
under-7500.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. Low-mileage drivers usually pay somewhat less.

over-15000.label: Over 15,000 miles a year
over-15000.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. High-mileage drivers usually pay somewhat more.

no.label: No good-student discount
no.derivation: The starting point for good student.

yes.label: Good-student discount (under 26)
yes.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. Many insurers offer a discount for a B average or better.

no.label: No driver-training discount
no.derivation: The starting point for driver training.

yes.label: Driver-training discount (under 22)
yes.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. Many insurers offer a discount for completing driver education.

multi-policy.title: Bundling
multi-policy.note: Home or renters policy with the same company.

yes.label: Bundled with a home or renters policy
yes.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. Most large insurers discount bundled policies.

area.title: Area
area.note: Where the car is kept. Rural is the starting point.

urban.label: Urban
urban.derivation: Same company and driver, city versus rural area. Oklahoma 2026: Oklahoma City and Tulsa versus Woodward and McAlester, all 10 profiles, median 1.163 (middle half of companies 1.079–1.272; 16%) over 800 comparisons. North Dakota 2026: Fargo versus "Remainder of State", Examples 1–3 and 5–12, median 0.987 (middle half of companies 0.886–1.070; -1%) over 228 comparisons. Value is the median of the two state medians.

suburban.label: Suburban
suburban.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. Halfway (on a multiplying scale) between the sourced rural and urban factors. The surveys we use compare cities with rural areas, not suburbs.

rural.label: Rural
rural.derivation: The starting point for area. Other areas are compared with it.

liability-limits.title: Liability limits
liability-limits.note: How much the policy pays others. Moves only the liability share.

100-300-100.label: 100/300/100 limits
100-300-100.derivation: The starting point for liability limits.

state-minimum.label: State-minimum liability limits
state-minimum.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. Lower limits cost less for the liability part of the premium. How much depends a lot on the state.

250-500-250.label: Higher limits (250/500/250)
250-500-250.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. Higher limits cost more for the liability part of the premium.

deductible.title: Deductible
deductible.note: What you pay first on a collision or comprehensive claim. Moves only the damage share.

500.label: $500 deductible
500.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. A lower deductible raises the collision and comprehensive part of the premium.

2000.label: $2,000 deductible
2000.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. A higher deductible lowers the collision and comprehensive part of the premium.

no.label: Owned outright
no.derivation: The starting point for loan or lease.

yes.label: Loan or lease (gap coverage)
yes.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. Lenders usually require collision and comprehensive, and many drivers add gap coverage.

vehicle-age.title: Vehicle age
vehicle-age.note: Years since the model year, counted from 2026. Moves only the damage share.

0-3.label: Vehicle 0–3 years old
0-3.derivation: The starting point for vehicle age.

4-7.label: Vehicle 4–7 years old
4-7.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. Older cars are worth less, so collision and comprehensive cost less.

8-12.label: Vehicle 8–12 years old
8-12.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. Older cars are worth less, so collision and comprehensive cost less.

13-plus.label: Vehicle 13 or more years old
13-plus.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. Older cars are worth less, so collision and comprehensive cost less.

premium-split.title: How a full-coverage premium splits
premium-split.note: Shares, not multipliers. Vehicle, limit, and deductible factors only move their own share.

liability.label: Liability share of a full-coverage premium
liability.derivation: ISO 2024 paid-claim frequency × severity, as published by the Insurance Information Institute: bodily injury 226.22, property damage 169.25, collision 228.34, comprehensive 91.09 dollars per car-year. Liability (bodily injury + property damage) is 55.3% of the four. Rough because these are loss costs, not prices, and leave out uninsured-motorist, medical, and PIP coverage. The low and high edges are our estimate; help wanted.

collision-in-physical.label: Collision share of collision + comprehensive
collision-in-physical.derivation: ISO 2024 paid-claim frequency × severity, as published by the Insurance Information Institute: bodily injury 226.22, property damage 169.25, collision 228.34, comprehensive 91.09 dollars per car-year. Collision ÷ (collision + comprehensive). Used to weight HLDI's collision and comprehensive results for a vehicle.

bodily-injury-in-liability.label: Bodily-injury share of liability
bodily-injury-in-liability.derivation: ISO 2024 paid-claim frequency × severity, as published by the Insurance Information Institute: bodily injury 226.22, property damage 169.25, collision 228.34, comprehensive 91.09 dollars per car-year. Bodily injury ÷ (bodily injury + property damage). Used to weight HLDI's bodily-injury and property-damage results for a vehicle.

range.title: How wide the range is
range.note: Not multipliers. Each one says how much less or more a real price could be when that thing changes.

typical-start.label: Starting from a typical price instead of your own
typical-start.derivation: How far companies' prices sit from the middle company for the same driver, car, and place: each premium ÷ the median premium for that profile and place (groups of 5 or more companies). Oklahoma 2026 and North Dakota 2026; median of the two states' 25th and 75th percentiles; 2140 premiums.

vehicle-model.label: How closely a company's price follows HLDI losses for a model
vehicle-model.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. Insurers rate vehicles with their own symbols. Those follow loss experience, but not exactly.

vehicle-model-years.label: Model year outside HLDI's years
vehicle-model-years.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. HLDI's results are for 2022–24 models; an older or newer design may differ.

vehicle-class.label: Using a class average instead of the exact model
vehicle-class.derivation: How far the HLDI series we keep sit from their class average, full-coverage weighting: 25th and 75th percentiles over 310 series.

vehicle-unknown.label: Vehicle not recognized
vehicle-unknown.derivation: How far the HLDI series we keep sit from the all-vehicle average (100), full-coverage weighting: 25th and 75th percentiles over 314 series.

trim-limited.label: Car version only partly matched
trim-limited.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. We are not sure which version of the car it is.

trim-unresolved.label: Car version not found
trim-unresolved.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. We could not find which version of the car it is.

state-unknown.label: Moving to a state without a typical price
state-unknown.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. Average prices differ a lot between states.

state-typical.label: Moving between states with typical prices
state-typical.derivation: Our estimate. No public source yet; help wanted. A state's typical price moves differently for different drivers.

vehicle.note: HLDI insurance losses for 2022–24 models, 100 = the average vehicle. Collision and comprehensive move only the damage share of the premium; property-damage and bodily-injury liability move only the liability share. When we don't have the exact model, we use the class average.
